title: Bench vice used by George Stephenson at Rainhill
summary: The iron bench vice is tied to Stephenson’s work during the Rainhill trials of 1829.
limit: Knowing who used a workholder does not show that they made it or identify every piece it held.
commonAction: Bring the flat practice block to the common jaw mark.
commonResult: The registered block rests flat. Its recorded tool-user tag stays separate from its maker line.
fittedAction: Add the soft edge pad for the angled wooden blank.
fittedResult: The fitted pad holds the blank’s corner without a fabricated maker’s stamp.
returnEvidence: Hesper inherited a clamp that fits the new block. Its earlier user is known. The maker line remains empty.
bench: Set out the repeatable jaw mark under its usable scope.
tray: Give the apprentice the fitted angled pad and record its limits.

title: Anvil from the Portslade forge
artDescription: Original schematic of the anvil’s long working face, tapered horn and foot.
summary: This anvil survives as one object from a set of tools associated with the Portslade forge in Sussex.
limit: A place association does not determine who performed a particular repair.
commonAction: Set the flat paper blank over the floor block outline.
commonResult: The work has a stable face. The pencilled owner field remains open.
fittedAction: Fit the curved scrap to the paper support shoe.
fittedResult: The curved scrap gains support with a separate work note.
returnEvidence: Hesper wants to credit the workshop without assigning a repair to an unrecorded hand.
bench: Leave a commonplace flat support with the proven shop name.
tray: Reserve the shaped cradle with a separate blank for its repairer.

title: Ron Hickman’s second Workmate prototype
summary: The prototype precedes the Workmate combined workbench and vice. Hickman’s account links the resemblance between the work-surface beams and separate vice jaws to his design.
limit: The prototype records one step in redesign. It does not stand for every later model.
commonAction: Close the common paper frame around the straight blank.
commonResult: The two model beams now hold a matched part and still support it.
fittedAction: Move the stop to hold an irregular model blank in a separate cradle.
fittedResult: The tailored stop keeps the edge supported without treating it as the standard blank.
returnEvidence: A porter can take a repeatable hold in one trip. A differently shaped part still needs its own fixture.
bench: Leave the common jaws ready for a repeated workshop job.
tray: Set the adapted tray apart for the irregular assembly.

title: Garrett saw bench safety-guard model
artDescription: Original silhouette of the historical model, with a raised guard and a bench on legs.
summary: The 1:4 study model shows a saw bench fitted with a safety guard. The catalogue links this to the British Factory Acts and factory inspection.
limit: The record is a historical model. No live tool is fitted or safety-certified in play.
commonAction: Put the painted warning shield before the card slot.
commonResult: The worker can find the intended hand position on the outside of the shield.
fittedAction: Fit a second shield with a lower receipt opening.
fittedResult: The poster remains visible at the low intake. The response strip has a distinct space.
returnEvidence: Hesper can close an obviously untested demonstration bay or arrange a locally witnessed practice route for one handled paper plate.
bench: Keep the clear outer boundary and its named stop.
tray: Keep the tailored paper station and offer a witnessed turn.

title: Compass plane for concave surfaces
artDescription: Original schematic of the plane’s curved wooden body and angled iron.
summary: The catalogue identifies this dated compass plane with smoothing concave surfaces.
limit: A plane that suits a curved patch cannot establish the fit of a flat joint.
commonAction: Slide the flat practice piece across the common guide.
commonResult: The straight form sits square in the frame. Its edge does not cover the curve marks.
fittedAction: Set the concave paper piece in its own shaped guide.
fittedResult: The practice model now touches the curve line without flattening it.
returnEvidence: The apprentice has a curved handle and a flat case side. A support for one leaves the other part still to check.
bench: Keep the standard flat fixture available for the next straight piece.
tray: Leave a curved support with a clearly named purpose.

title: D. Malloch & Son smoothing plane
summary: The SMG record names D. Malloch & Son of Perth and lists the item as a smoothing plane.
limit: A smooth visible face alone cannot show whether a deep joint or hidden return was fitted.
commonAction: Put the face strip against the regular viewing reference.
commonResult: The surface can be compared in the stance used for this practice trial.
fittedAction: Put the small edge template next to the hidden return.
fittedResult: The outer face and the tucked-around edge have their own witness marks.
returnEvidence: Hesper can let someone check the visible surface while marking where the deeper fit still needs an edge witness.
bench: Leave the steady face guide with one scoped reading.
tray: Set aside a tailored return template for the deeper check.

title: One-half model of a segmental turning lathe
summary: The model illustrates a type of lathe used where a part did not need or could not make a full turn.
limit: A partial move can explain its useful arc while leaving the rest of a whole turn untested.
commonAction: Put the straight training piece onto the common turning diagram.
commonResult: The drawing covers a full circle for the dummy piece with no raised corner.
fittedAction: Set the stop at the two ends of the model’s shorter arc.
fittedResult: This irregular model moves between marked ends. The rest of its circle remains outside the checked movement.
returnEvidence: The work bench can demonstrate a known full-turn example or keep a shorter-motion support for the piece that needs it.
bench: Open the full-turn practice station for the regular model.
tray: Give the learner the two separate limits on the fitted short arc.

title: Regnard Frères’s one-fifth copying lathe model
summary: This Paris model reproduces a copying lathe at 1:5 scale. The model records an approach to repeat shapes.
limit: Matching a copied outline does not verify the internal fit, material or size of a full product.
commonAction: Put the master outline next to the first miniature contour.
commonResult: The two paper outlines meet at the named scale. The shared original is tagged.
fittedAction: Set a sectional sample into the special slot under the copy.
fittedResult: The section adds an independent check for a place the outline cannot show.
returnEvidence: Hesper needs to let a second workshop reproduce an outline without promising identical interiors.
bench: Pass on the marked common outline and its scale.
tray: Keep the independently checked section with the fitted copy.

title: Set of Johansson gauge blocks
summary: This imperial set contains eighty-one gauge blocks in an oak case.
limit: A repeatable reference length cannot give a calibrated result if the unit or blocks used are missing from its record.
commonAction: Set two fixed paper measures together inside the standard-length sleeve.
commonResult: The practice length has an inch reference and a recorded pair of starting marks.
fittedAction: Fit the case-specific step block and write its separate unit mark.
fittedResult: The new register checks a different local stopping point while keeping its reference name.
returnEvidence: Hesper has two gauge examples from different suppliers. Keep which unit the worker actually used next to the usable length.
bench: Put one repeatable length on the common fixture bench.
tray: Leave the fitted step and its separate unit in the apprentice tray.

title: J. Gilmour’s error-compensating height gauge
summary: The Science Museum Group records a height gauge that compensates for error and has its accessories in a wooden box.
limit: The claim of compensation still needs a baseline, and a changed support can introduce a new error.
commonAction: Set the empty model gauge against the independent fixed foot.
commonResult: Both use the same plane at the zero check; the empty reading is recoverable.
fittedAction: Test the adjusted dummy on a separate sloping support.
fittedResult: The witness strip shows which offset belongs to the support and which to the dummy.
returnEvidence: The two-height practice blank looks alike when someone measures from the wrong foot. Hesper leaves the reference visible for the next try.
bench: Keep the zero reference with the common base line.
tray: Offer the separately fitted support for an offset check.

title: Rowi Model 1 slide mounting jig
summary: The museum records a jig for mounting photographic slides, with its box and printed instructions.
limit: A slide can fit a mount while its viewing direction still needs to be checked.
commonAction: Set the square study mount against the common corner stop.
commonResult: The image card sits within the square opening. The direction is not yet known.
fittedAction: Fit a separate corner locator to the asymmetric image card.
fittedResult: The locator gives the viewer a reference for the correct upright view.
returnEvidence: Hesper can pass the common opening to the label-maker, or offer the corner placement so the printed orientation can be repeated.
bench: Leave the standard square frame with a direction note.
tray: Set the keyed corner in the display drawer.

title: Henry Maudslay’s small “Lord Chancellor” micrometer
summary: Maudslay’s workshops used a bench micrometer for disputed measurements. The catalogue suggests this small example may have helped plan a larger one.
limit: Its name and form are documented. The identification as a planning model is a possibility rather than a certainty.
commonAction: Put a plain reference bar beneath the model pointer.
commonResult: The bar reads the same at both indicated spaces on the standard foot.
fittedAction: Set the possible larger outline on a separate model board.
fittedResult: The outline carries its question mark without changing the verified measurement.
returnEvidence: The apprentice wants to call the old tool the final referee. Hesper keeps a checked reference and an open catalogue line separately.
bench: Fix the plain reference where it can be checked again.
tray: Put the tentative scale and resizing note beside the later model.

title: Whitworth’s millionth measuring machine
summary: The machine compared standard inch bars. The catalogue says temperature affects its performance and reports that the National Physical Laboratory rejected Whitworth’s claimed precision.
limit: This tool and its recorded claim do not establish accuracy to a millionth of an inch.
commonAction: Place the two paper standards side by side at the shared baseline.
commonResult: The study scale reads an equal reference while both bars have the same condition tag.
fittedAction: Set a changed room strip beside the fixed standard.
fittedResult: The altered strip moves by one marked division in this fictional model. The printed claim is now narrower.
returnEvidence: Hesper offers one comparison under a named condition. A second practitioner can leave an open slot for a future check.
bench: Post the single checked comparison and its shared condition.
tray: Leave the two condition strips and a clear place for a witness.

title: Moore & Wright Braille micrometer
summary: Moore & Wright worked with the Royal National Institute for the Blind to develop this Braille micrometer design in the 1950s.
limit: Accessible reading methods should preserve the same reference and unit, without assuming every user reads by the same sense.
commonAction: Line up the ordinary large-mark and raised-mark samples on the same zero.
commonResult: Both representations carry the same practice starting point.
fittedAction: Offer the offset-fitted reading frame at the lower table.
fittedResult: The reader can reach the raised copy and independently check its shared unit.
returnEvidence: The apprentice’s work is only promised to be readable after a user tries it. Keep the same common zero as the access changes.
bench: Leave a shared visible and raised reference at the regular bench.
tray: Offer a reachable fitted holder for a separate repeat.

title: Alan Pedder’s apprenticeship toolbox
summary: Pedder used these tools during engineering training at Associated Electrical Industries in Trafford Park. He made some of the tools himself.
limit: Tool ownership and use do not mean every item in the set was made by the apprentice.
commonAction: Put the apprentice’s name on the dated whole-box label.
commonResult: The tray links to the training period. Individual maker fields remain separate.
fittedAction: Fit the separately supported making record into the open tool slot.
fittedResult: One item now has a specific role while the rest stay within the whole-box scope.
returnEvidence: Hesper wants excellent work to show up in the apprentice’s record while keeping others’ labour visible too.
bench: Leave the broad apprenticeship reference on the public bench.
tray: Place the particular credited tool and its separate witness in the tray.

title: W. Crosland’s pattern-book swatch guillotine
summary: W. Crosland made this device in Bredbury. Allsops used it to cut paper and fabric samples for pattern books.
limit: Uniform sample size does not make every fabric or colour equivalent.
commonAction: Seat the two imitation paper swatches in the same viewing window.
commonResult: Both samples fit the standard aperture. Their textures still have distinct labels.
fittedAction: Put the fabric sample comparison in its own holder below the light strip.
fittedResult: The different surface stays noticeable under a matched viewing condition.
returnEvidence: The earlier bench can distribute samples that fit a folder while keeping which surface they preserve.
bench: Leave the shared window and keep the surface descriptions.
tray: Offer the independent surface sample board to a waiting maker.

title: Holtzapffel set of eighteen screw-thread plug gauges
summary: The London set contains gauges for the Holtzapffel system identified by sizes D to U.
limit: A candidate part can fit the intended system and still require a different reference in another workshop.
commonAction: Set the marked paper gauge in the master row.
commonResult: It drops in the intended practice opening. The system name remains on its side.
fittedAction: Fit the off-system piece in a separately adapted holder.
fittedResult: The second model needs its own reference sheet. It did not pass through the original opening.
returnEvidence: A visitor from another guild brings a part measured against a different named system. Hesper can compare both gauges without combining their marks.
bench: Leave the keyed standard row in open view.
tray: Make space for a separately labelled other-system fit.

title: Japanese saw set
summary: The record identifies this mid-nineteenth-century saw set as made in Japan. It does not name an individual maker.
limit: The tool category identifies its intended task. The plate alone does not identify a specific workshop or type of finished cut.
commonAction: Put a straight printed edge in the common profile stool.
commonResult: The model shows a checked edge view. The workshop attribution is still unspecified.
fittedAction: Set a practice zigzag profile in the side cradle.
fittedResult: A different profile keeps its own line, away from the smooth reference.
returnEvidence: Hesper can help a learner describe profiles without adding an unsupported claim about who produced the object.
bench: Display the general edge profile by itself and leave its maker open.
tray: Bring the separate model profile and its working scope to the side table.

title: Bob Watkins’s apprentice-made thread gauge
summary: The gauge was used to measure thread pitch. Watkins made it as an apprentice in the mid-1960s.
limit: A pitch check alone does not identify how a whole fastener fits or who made it.
commonAction: Fit the spaced paper marks under the common counting window.
commonResult: Several ticks share the verified spacing inside the window.
fittedAction: Retain a second cross-section in the deeper fitted support.
fittedResult: The full dummy fits differently once its width is checked. The pitch reading remains valid.
returnEvidence: Hesper needs to show which simple match was checked, so the next worker knows when to check the rest of the part.
bench: Leave the repeatable spacing reference and its date.
tray: Add a named second-width check with the fitted dummy.

title: Henry Bowker’s carriage-builder tool chest
summary: The record connects the chest, contents and paperwork to Henry Bowker, who worked at Duckinfield Wagon Works and York Carriageworks.
limit: A chest and its papers can link a job, owner or place without making them one provenance entry.
commonAction: Put the paper chest card above its common ownership label.
commonResult: The owner remains visible while the working-location fields have separate slots.
fittedAction: Lay a copy of the small location tag by its own compartment.
fittedResult: A venue can be named with a distinct document. The other workshop remains indexed separately.
returnEvidence: Hesper wants the owner recorded while keeping which place each shop slip actually covers.
bench: Leave the shared owner index in the common tray.
tray: Fit both location tags beside the documents that support them.

title: John Stirrup’s carpenter’s tool chest
summary: The chest has drawers and internal boxes catalogued separately. The museum associates its making with John Stirrup around 1830.
limit: The maker named on the chest does not determine who made each individual tool stored inside it.
commonAction: Put the main chest title in the shared open drawer.
commonResult: The main object title remains clear. Later parts and contents stay in the index.
fittedAction: Bring the internal box tag to a fitted paper compartment.
fittedResult: The contents remain tied to a precise position, through the smaller sub-record.
returnEvidence: Hesper can show the whole box to a new reader. The inventory clerk needs a place they can name for the small compartment.
bench: Open the common main-catalogue layout.
tray: Give the small tagged compartment its own fitted tray.

title: Pierre Dubreuil’s oil print The Tool Chest
summary: The photograph is an oil print mounted on paper and titled The Tool Chest.
limit: A picture of a chest can reveal an arrangement in its frame. It does not inventory any closed drawers.
commonAction: Put the printed view against its standard aperture.
commonResult: The outer form stays visible. The inside ledger is still empty.
fittedAction: Raise an independent drawn drawer tab next to the photograph.
fittedResult: The tab gets a separate source box instead of being added to the photographic frame.
returnEvidence: The old bench picture guides a learner to the place a box stood. The missing contents still belong in their own evidence slot.
bench: Leave the framed view with the boundary named.
tray: Mount the separately sourced drawer card in the fitting tray.

title: Hirata SCARA workholder and control cabinets
artDescription: Original schematic with the robot on its workholding stand beside two control cabinets.
summary: The museum records an industrial robot on a stand with a workholding device and two control cabinets.
limit: The item list documents components. It does not establish that later workshop setups or controls were identical.
commonAction: Place the standard cardboard part in the marked workholder.
commonResult: The travelling card can follow its repeated path when the part matches the frame.
fittedAction: Fit a second support for the practice part with the off-centre edge.
fittedResult: The operator has to keep the support label and changed path distinct.
returnEvidence: Hesper can teach a repeatable movement or mark the newly fitted support as a different setup in the workshop record.
bench: Keep the common path with the straight-card fixture.
tray: Leave the fitted support and its separate path with a witness.

title: Joseph Finney’s dial micrometer
summary: This micrometer reads changes in a brass bar as part of a temperature-indicating device.
limit: An observed change in length is a proxy for temperature in its specific tool, with assumptions about the bar and reference.
commonAction: Mount the straight sample against the standard marker.
commonResult: The model points to the measured separation. Its readout alone gives no material key.
fittedAction: Place the named material and temperature label beside the same study mark.
fittedResult: The link is readable through the fixture’s chosen comparison model.
returnEvidence: A student using the gauge can name what the pointer directly shows, and what depends on the inference kept beside it.
bench: Hand over the common separation mark to the open bench.
tray: Give the fitted material key to the apprentice’s tray.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: John William Jarboe’s photographic plate vise
artDescription: Original exterior schematic of Jarboe’s 1857 patented design, with a long wooden base, two low jaws and a raised handle. The surviving model’s finish is unverified here.
summary: The Smithsonian catalogues this photographic plate vise as Jarboe’s patent model. The illustration follows the exterior in his 1857 patent drawing. The surviving model’s finish is unverified here.
limit: A holder can demonstrate consistent placement. The patent object itself does not supply an image or record of exposure.
commonAction: Put the blank card flat into the practice plate guide.
commonResult: The corners register against the standard stops. The imaginary image field stays blank.
fittedAction: Place a narrower photographic dummy in the adapted guide.
fittedResult: The auxiliary support keeps the edge from turning while preserving the same named viewpoint.
returnEvidence: Hesper can show a reusable plate holder without claiming the pictured result came from it.
bench: Offer the simple position stop in the common workspace.
tray: Fit the small plate’s separate support in the apprentice tray.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: Emory A. Angell’s loom temple patent model
artDescription: Original silhouette of the patent model’s long metal plate and raised centre.
date: Before 19 October 1838; patent issued that day
summary: The record associates this loom temple model with patent number 987, issued to Angell in 1838.
limit: A patent model illustrates an intended solution. It does not measure how widely a design was used.
commonAction: Lay the narrow paper cloth length along the bench’s standard guides.
commonResult: The practice strip stays within its intended parallel guide marks.
fittedAction: Fit the second holder for the wider cloth strip.
fittedResult: A different cloth width gains its own support. The original model and patent date stay named.
returnEvidence: One fabric order needs a known setup. A second customer arrives with wider cloth and needs its own check.
bench: Leave the shared width guide ready for repeats.
tray: Offer the tested wider support and record the extra condition.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: Josiah Lyman’s triangular drafting-scale patent model
summary: The German silver triangular rule carries different marked faces. The record distinguishes the maker mark and the scales.
limit: The same drawn length can stand for different distances under two named scales.
commonAction: Align the common scale face to the fixed printed footmark.
commonResult: One line carries the selected scale and interval together.
fittedAction: Turn the model to its second faced ruler and compare with the same printed origin.
fittedResult: The drawn length has not moved. The number has its own scale context.
returnEvidence: Two workers in Emberford brought copies that look alike. One worker still needs the face identifier to know what the number means.
bench: Post the measured drawing with the chosen scale face.
tray: Keep both rule faces and their independent key in a fitted tray.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: John Mischker’s reversible micrometer
summary: The mechanism has a reversible and adjustable measuring spindle, or gauge member.
limit: Changing how a gauge sits can change its reference. A match in one orientation does not check the other.
commonAction: Seat the model pointer in the standard first position.
commonResult: The printed mark is aligned with a clear fixed base.
fittedAction: Turn the reversible study marker and fit its different zero key.
fittedResult: The change in orientation is recorded on the second reference, even when the shape looks unchanged.
returnEvidence: The apprentice can repeat a known orientation or try the reversed view with its own check.
bench: Fix one clearly named orientation in the common slot.
tray: Leave both orientations and a fitted zero key with the next worker.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: Abijah S. Hosley’s ship-model measurer patent model
summary: The caliper model accompanied a patent application. Its catalogue description explains the use of wooden models made to separate into pieces.
limit: A profile checked on one model slice does not establish the section shapes elsewhere or on a completed ship.
commonAction: Set the paper section into the common measuring holder.
commonResult: One named section rests on the origin line. The other section remains unchecked.
fittedAction: Fit the other section to its separate place mark.
fittedResult: A second width can be compared from the same kind of stand, with its own location.
returnEvidence: Hesper can show a regular cross-section on the bench or keep a fitted stop for the piece that leaves the original line.
bench: Keep the named checked section by the shared reference.
tray: Put the separately fitted section and location marker in the tray.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: William Patrick’s gage-lathe patent model
summary: The museum identifies this as a patent model for a woodworking lathe, with painted bed and treadle.
limit: A painted feature can help explain the model’s parts without establishing its real production rate.
commonAction: Fit the coloured bed drawing beside its common feed marker.
commonResult: The parts can be pointed to and repeated in this fixed model.
fittedAction: Put the changed-profile dummy into a fitted support.
fittedResult: The special piece retains its own setup tag apart from the original model.
returnEvidence: Hesper can teach the original arrangement at the main bench and leave proof of performance for another worker to test.
bench: Post one model finding with its intended scope.
tray: Keep the fitted piece and the open performance card together.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: A. H. Wood’s engraver’s vice patent model
summary: The Smithsonian describes a vise intended to hold the plate firmly with a yielding work surface.
limit: Firm holding and a surface that gives slightly can serve different parts of a task. Neither is a general quality verdict.
commonAction: Put a flat dummy into the fixed support and check its edge label.
commonResult: The flat piece stays steady, but the supporting surface condition is unknown.
fittedAction: Add the separate compliant paper support to the model.
fittedResult: The edge is held while the marked face can move by its listed amount in the exercise.
returnEvidence: One job needs a fast rigid hold while a second needs a check on how the softer support treats its face.
bench: Leave the common edge holder and its stated limit.
tray: Keep the fitted face support at the smaller witness table.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: Luman Carpenter’s ellipsographic copying-machine patent model
summary: The catalogue identifies a model for cutting repeated forms using a common pattern.
limit: Multiple copies can share the same error if they come from one pattern.
commonAction: Put the common pattern over two study outlines.
commonResult: Both copies follow the same mark. The shared source stays visible.
fittedAction: Bring an independent template on a different colour of paper.
fittedResult: A comparison shape escapes the common copying error on the small practice plate.
returnEvidence: Hesper wants the worker to keep the template’s origin with each repeated copy.
bench: Offer the two copies with a single, explicitly shared source label.
tray: Fit the independent cross-check at the small proving stand.

title: Seventeenth-century rabbet plane
summary: The Met identifies this multi-part object as a rabbet plane and retains its component identifiers.
limit: A catalogue part number can guide retrieval. It does not establish that an imitation fits a particular historical joint.
commonAction: Open the stepped paper section against the ordinary corner guide.
commonResult: The step is visible and its check stays on the same face.
fittedAction: Fit the second pattern into a deeper model section.
fittedResult: A different edge fit is clear after the section is opened.
returnEvidence: Hesper can explain the step along a standard diagram or let the apprentice check how a deeper joint works in the study jig.
bench: Leave the common section in sight at the shared bench.
tray: Put the separate deeper guide in the named fitted tray.

title: William Henry Fox Talbot’s Carpenter and Apprentice
summary: The photograph depicts a carpenter and apprentice. The museum comments on how the paper negative renders form and shaded planes.
limit: The image shows one appearance and arrangement. It does not record every motion of the work or the apprentice’s own account.
commonAction: Set the paper photograph in the common angled window.
commonResult: The visible frame makes the broad shapes easy to compare. The unseen actions remain open.
fittedAction: Add the separately signed activity strip to the small fitted clip.
fittedResult: The two records answer different questions about the same model work.
returnEvidence: The apprentice is seen in a working picture. Hesper wants their experience to have its own record as well.
bench: Leave the picture with its scope line at the public bench.
tray: File the picture and independently witnessed work at different slots.

title: Template and tools from the D’Angelico Workshop
summary: The Met identifies this accession as a template and tools from the D’Angelico Workshop.
limit: A surviving template documents one working reference. It does not establish that each resulting instrument sounded or fitted identically.
commonAction: Put the shared outline over a dummy soundboard panel.
commonResult: The profile matches the stencil, keeping a separate blank for the sound test.
fittedAction: Set the side-profile pattern in its separate witness jack.
fittedResult: The small edge check adds a piece of evidence outside the outline alone.
returnEvidence: A maker has promised that instruments from the same outline sound alike. A checked edge and shared pattern do not give that listening record.
bench: Keep the shared outline with the promise narrowed to the visible cut.
tray: Leave a separately fitted frame and an open slot for heard evidence.

title: Foil cutting plate from Tiffany Studios
summary: The Met attributes this foil cutting plate to Tiffany Studios and dates it to 1900–07.
limit: A sourced cutting plate preserves a workshop form. It cannot identify the exact hand or workshop object produced by it without another record.
commonAction: Put the pattern plate in the shared grid’s fixed corner.
commonResult: Its profile falls within the common grid. The next owner field is empty.
fittedAction: Fit the photographed comparison on a distinct receipt slot.
fittedResult: A second paper record can support a match without turning the cutting plate into its own witness.
returnEvidence: Hesper can let the tracing station use a repeatable profile or keep an independently named comparison piece.
bench: Pass on the common grid and scoped cut outline.
tray: Keep the separate proof panel with its own source note.

title: Ryūryūkyo Shinsai’s Tools for the Carpenter
summary: This dated Japanese print depicts tools associated with carpentry.
limit: A selected display of tools is evidence about a representation. It is not an inventory of all Japanese carpenters’ practices.
commonAction: Fit the separate captions along the printing model.
commonResult: The kit is pictured together. Only the visibly selected tools receive captions.
fittedAction: Place a separate working tool record in a fitted reader’s tray.
fittedResult: The source line now separates the print’s representation from the independent equipment record.
returnEvidence: Hesper’s picture names a selection of the shop objects. The record for a separate tool needs its own place and source.
bench: Leave just the dated print with its visible selection.
tray: Mount the independent tool record at the fitted viewing table.

title: Twelfth-century pottery mold
summary: The Met records this earthenware mold as excavated at Nishapur and proposes a bowl or part of a jug as possible results.
limit: A mold can preserve an intended repeated shape. It does not establish the identity of an individual vessel without a separate match.
commonAction: Put the paper inverse shape over a practice impression.
commonResult: The two outlines correspond when the face is named.
fittedAction: Fit another pressed shape into the separate test drawer.
fittedResult: A small difference survives despite the shared broad outline.
returnEvidence: The apprentice can repeat a shared form or examine whether a particular impression has sufficient independent evidence.
bench: Give the standard shape to the common pattern bench.
tray: Fit the separately checked impression into the small witness drawer.

title: Mold with unfired frit still present
summary: The Met identifies this mold by the presence of unfired frit and dates it to Egypt’s New Kingdom.
limit: An unfired remainder shows an unfinished material state. It does not prove a finished ornament was successfully made with this specimen.
commonAction: Place the labelled unfinished material card beside the common mold outline.
commonResult: A visible remainder has its own state before the model’s later stage.
fittedAction: Compare a separately sourced finished outline in the fitted tray.
fittedResult: The completed shape comes from its own illustration. The leftover material remains unfired in the record.
returnEvidence: The workshop’s practice tray holds some unfinished material on one side. A finished sample should get its own label and source.
bench: Leave the unfinished state attached to the common drawing.
tray: Add the independently sourced comparison with its fitted tray.

title: John Jennion’s toolmaker trade card
summary: The British Museum identifies this anonymous trade card with Jennion’s shop. Its design shows three planes and a border of other tools.
limit: The sign advertises a shop and its trade. It does not prove that one exact tool was sold or used by a named customer.
commonAction: Put the shop emblem in the shared sign frame.
